spec.title: PROP-077 — Weak dependencies for every package kind: `[recommends]` on applications and the general `--no-recommends`
spec.p: Framework record, owner decision 2026-11-10, settled against the tree at `ef8e9c312`. The decision is one sentence of the owner's: **an application package may recommend other vibe applications — Java recommends maven, Node recommends pnpm — and they are installed when they are installable; and there is one general `--no-recommends` for every package kind, projects included, where today no such flag exists anywhere.** This document exists rather than an amendment of PROP-075 because the subject is the general package model and not template packages: PROP-075 `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS` is the sibling decision about an author's recommended *ecosystem* items, a different layer with a different installer, and the two meet only in the flag. The model the decision extends is PROP-003 §2.3's libsolv/RPM weak-dependency level set (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/modules/vibe-resolver/PROP-003#CAP-RECOMMENDS`, `#CAP-SUGGESTS`, `#CAP-WEAK-DEPS-MAPPING`, `#CAP-WEAK-DEPS-WARNING`); nothing of that model's meaning changes here, only how far it reaches and how a user declines it. Implementation is phase **P7d** of `campaigns/app-versions-2026-11/PLAN.md`; every fact below is `spec/plan` except the one that records what already ships.

p.WEAK-PURPOSE: A package author can say "this is almost always wanted beside me" once, and it holds wherever the package is installed. `vibe install -g org.example.java/jdk` brings maven; `vibe install -g org.vibevm.node/node` brings pnpm; a project dependency keeps behaving as it does today. A user who does not want the companions says `--no-recommends`, one flag, the same spelling for a project install, a global application install and an update, and nothing is installed that the user did not either ask for or decline to decline. What the user does **not** get is a surprise that cannot be seen first: a recommendation appears in `--plan-only` and in the install report before and after it happens, and a recommendation that fails never fails the install the user actually asked for.

p.WEAK-TODAY: **What already ships, measured in the code rather than assumed, 2026-11-10.** `[recommends]` and `[suggests]` are parsed for every package-role manifest (`crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/package/weak_deps.rs`, `crates/vibe-core/src/manifest/document.rs`), and the resolver honours `[recommends]` on the **project** plane by a greedy best-effort expansion: after the hard solve, each recommended reference is tried by a re-solve and kept only if the graph stays satisfiable, a conflicting one is dropped silently, and an accepted one enters the graph as a requirement and never as a root (`crates/vibe-resolver/src/resolvo_engine/mod.rs`, `collect_recommends`; the same greedy policy in `crates/vibe-resolver/src/source_solve.rs`). `[suggests]` is read and ignored by the solver, as its level means. Two gaps, and they are exactly what this document closes: **there is no `--no-recommends` flag anywhere in the tree**, for any kind; and **the application plane never reads `[recommends]` at all**, because `vibe install -g` does not go through the dependency solver — it resolves exactly one package through `resolve_and_fetch` (`crates/vibe-app/src/resolve.rs`) and installs it. An application's companion today is expressible only as an installer feature inside the same package (PROP-065 `#features`) or as a step requirement (`#app-dependencies`), neither of which can name a separate product the user may later want to remove on its own. **Corrected 2026-11-10, after measuring the project plane end to end rather than at the solver seam:** the greedy expansion above is real and the recommended package does enter the solved graph, and the PROP-050 `#EFFECTIVE-SET` visibility projection then **prunes it again** — it is not a root and no manifest declares an edge to it, so `analyze` finds it unreachable and `prune_graph` drops it before anything is fetched, locked or materialised. So `[recommends]` has no observable effect on a project install today, by any route; what ships is the expansion, not the installation. That is recorded here rather than fixed by this phase, because admitting a weak graph member into a consumer's effective set is a PROP-050 decision and not a reach decision; `#P7D-AS-BUILT` states it as the one finding the phase did not act on.

p.APP-RECOMMENDS: **Decided 2026-11-10 — an application's `[recommends]` is honoured by the application installer, with the same meaning the level has everywhere.** When `vibe install -g` (or `vibe update -g`, or an application install into a project home under PROP-059 `#project-scope`) has installed a package **successfully and committed its record**, every reference in that package's `[recommends]` is installed by the same installer, best-effort, as an ordinary installation of its own. The declaration is the one that already exists — `[recommends] packages = ["group/name@req", …]`, the same table and the same `PackageRef` grammar the project plane reads — so an author writes one table, not one per plane, and a package that is installed both ways recommends the same things both ways. A reference the application plane cannot install is **reported and skipped, never a failure**: a package that is not `kind = "app"`, one with no installer option for this platform, one no configured registry carries, one whose requirement nothing satisfies, and one whose own installation fails each produce one report line naming the reference and the reason, and leave the exit status of the install the user asked for exactly as it was. That is `CAP-WEAK-DEPS-WARNING`'s "a warning, not an error" applied to the plane that had no implementation of it. A reference already satisfied by an installed version is skipped as satisfied and reported as such.

p.APP-RECOMMENDS-MECHANICS: **Decided 2026-11-10 — the loop, the order, the depth, and how the inventory remembers.** The installer keeps a visited set keyed by `(group, name)`, seeded with the package the user named, and walks **breadth-first in declaration order**: the requested package's recommendations first, in the order the table writes them, then the recommendations of each one that was installed. Transitive is deliberate and matches the project plane, where a recommended package's own recommends already ride the same expansion loop; the visited set is what makes it terminate, and there is no depth limit, because a limit would be a number nobody could justify while a cycle is already impossible. Each installation is the ordinary one — the ordinary resolution, the ordinary installer options, features and defaults, the ordinary record — run **after** the recommender's record is committed, so a failure can never leave the recommender half-installed; `--plan-only` resolves the whole walk and prints it as the plan's own subtree, one node per recommended package with its reason, downloading nothing. **The inventory records a weak edge, and that is the whole new state.** A recommended installation is recorded `auto` with the recommender as its requirer, exactly as a step requirement already is (PROP-065 `#uninstall-tree`), with one attribute distinguishing it: the edge is **weak**. A weak edge never blocks a removal in either direction — `vibe uninstall -g` of the recommender succeeds and reports what it leaves behind with the exact command to remove it, and `vibe uninstall -g` of the recommended package succeeds although the recommender is installed, because a recommendation the user has removed is a decision and not a broken dependency. An installation with no strong and no weak requirer left is an orphan and is offered to `vibe app autoremove` as orphans already are; an installation the user installed by name is `manual` and is never autoremoved, however many weak edges point at it. No new removal verb, no new prompt, no new document: one attribute on an edge the inventory already carries.

p.APP-RECOMMENDS-CONSENT: **Decided 2026-11-10 — no new consent gate, and why that is the honest answer here.** Installing a package is the consent to what that package declares (PROP-054 `##INSTALL-IS-CONSENT`, PROP-020 `#INSTALLATION-CONSENT-SUCCESSOR`), and a recommendation is a declaration. So the application installer asks nothing new: it prints what it will install before it installs it, in the plan and in the report, attended or not, and the opt-out is `--no-recommends` rather than a question. Two boundaries keep that from becoming an npm-style ambient install. First, a recommendation installs a **vibe package through the ordinary installer**, with its own record, its own uninstall and its own place in `vibe app list` — nothing is written outside the installer's own surfaces, and nothing becomes invisible. Second, the project plane's existing arbitrary-code consent gate is **not** weakened: an application installed into a project home still passes the allow-list and `--assume-yes` check it passes today (`crates/vibe-cli/src/commands/app/project.rs`), and a recommended package is checked by the same gate as the package that recommended it, so a recommendation cannot be a way past a consent the direct request would have needed.

p.NO-RECOMMENDS-FLAG: **Decided 2026-11-10 — `--no-recommends`, one flag for every kind.** It is a **global flag**, declared once beside `--offline` and `--refresh` rather than per command, because it answers one question — "may vibe install things I did not name?" — that reads the same on every plane. Where it is honoured: `vibe install` and `vibe update` of a project (the solver's greedy weak expansion is not run at all, so the solve is the hard solve and nothing else), `vibe install -g` / `vibe update -g` and an application install into a project home (the walk of `#APP-RECOMMENDS-MECHANICS` is not entered), `vibe reinstall` of either plane, and — because an author's recommendation is one idea with two spellings — the **ecosystem** recommendations of PROP-075 `#ECOSYSTEM-RECOMMENDS`, whose enabled items are treated as empty. On a command that neither solves nor installs, the flag is a **usage refusal naming it**, by the same mechanism that already refuses project-only flags to `vibe install -g`; a flag silently ignored is worse than a flag refused. **It changes a solve, never a replay.** A project's lock already records a recommended package as a non-root graph member, so `vibe install` with no arguments materialises exactly what the lock says and the flag has nothing to do there — which is why **no lock field, no inventory field and no epoch step is needed for the flag itself**, and why a user cannot produce the flapping a recorded preference would cause. A later deliberate re-solve (`vibe update`) re-applies whichever way the flag is passed then, and the diff it writes is visible in the lock like any other. **Rejected: a `--with-recommends`.** Recommendations are on by default, as the level means and as the owner decided; a flag that re-asserts the default is surface with no question behind it. **Rejected: a persisted `[install] recommends = false` user setting** — not because it is wrong, but because it is a second place for one answer and nothing asked for it yet; the flag comes first and a setting can follow it under the ordinary `~/.vibe/config.toml` `[install]` table if a user ever asks.

p.SUGGESTS-UNCHANGED: **Decided 2026-11-10 — `[suggests]` gains a voice and no behaviour.** The level means "never auto-installed", and that does not change on any plane: the solver keeps ignoring it and the application installer never reads it as something to install. What it gains is the one thing a hint is for — being seen: `vibe install`, `vibe install -g` and their updates report the suggestions of the packages they installed, once, as a trailing line naming each reference, and `--json` carries them beside the recommendations that were installed and the ones that were skipped. `--no-recommends` does not silence them, because they install nothing; the ordinary log level does. Nothing is resolved to produce the line — it is read from the manifests already in hand, so a suggestion of a package no registry carries still prints, which is exactly what a hint may be.

p.WEAK-FORMAT-CHANGES: **Decided 2026-11-10.** The surfaces this document touches are recorded in the campaign's own change log, `campaigns/app-versions-2026-11/FORMAT-CHANGES.md`, under the ids `AV-FMT-030` (the flag and the application plane's reading of `[recommends]`, with the install report's `recommended[]` / `skipped[]` / `suggested[]` members) and `AV-FMT-029` (the application inventory's weak requirer edge, which rides the same protocol step as the campaign's other inventory additions rather than taking one of its own). No manifest field is added at all: `[recommends]` and `[suggests]` already exist and already parse for every kind, which is the strongest evidence that this is a reach decision and not a grammar decision. The regime is the campaign's — `formats/EPOCHS.toml` `public = false`, `break_window_open = true` — so no break note is required.

p.P7D-AS-BUILT: **Implemented 2026-11-10 (campaign phase P7d) — what the code decided that this document left open, plus the one finding the phase did not act on.** Nine amendments. **(1) The inventory generation is paid here, not by P7c.** The plan said whichever of P7c and P7d landed first owns the `[format.application-index]` **6 → 7** move, the `vibe-user-applications/8` tag and the `vibe-app-proxy` admission PROP-059 `#proxy-index-upgrade` requires; P7d landed first and paid all three. The new generation's only addition is `weak` on a `requirement` row, so the writer's ladder gains one rung and nothing else: a home that holds no recommendation goes on writing `/7` — or `/6`, or `/3` — and every existing PATH proxy goes on reading it, which is the whole reason the generation costs nothing. **What P7c inherits** is therefore an `e7` schema already registered with its corpus, the frozen `[format.application-index-v7]` reader beside `/3`…`/6`, an `e6 → e7` promotion that fabricates no weak edge, and a proxy that admits `/8`: the per-adapter extras record of `AV-FMT-029` is added as **optional members of this same `e7` generation at epoch 7 → 7**, with no further protocol move, and the one code change it owes is a clause in `Index::requires_reader_eight`, which is written as the ladder's rung rather than as the weak edge's own predicate for exactly that reason. **(2) `required_by` had to answer weakness, because the three readers of a reverse edge want different things of it.** A weak edge keeps its target **out** of the orphan set and blocks a removal in **neither** direction, so one boolean reverse edge could not serve both; `Index::required_by` now answers a `ReverseEdge { owner, scope, weak }`, and an owner that records both a requirement and a recommendation of one target is **not** weak — the strong edge decides. **(3) A recommendation that is already installed still records the edge.** `#APP-RECOMMENDS` says a satisfied reference is «skipped as satisfied and reported as such», which read literally would record nothing; as built the weak edge is recorded for a reference that ends up **present**, installed by this walk or already there, because the recommender's `requires` list is rewritten from its plan on every install and a second `install -g` of the recommender would otherwise drop the edge and orphan the companion. The walk itself nevertheless **stops** at a present reference, as the fact's literal reading says and as the plan stops: `--plan-only` must be the whole truth about the walk, and three things fall out of the same rule — a resolution of a package nothing will install is not paid, an already-installed companion's own `requires` list is not rewritten by its recommender's install so nothing below it is lost, and a `--no-recommends` the user spent on the companion's own install is not undone later by installing something that recommends it. **(4) The walk's own publication needs the proxy image.** The weak edge is the first thing in a home that needs the `/8` reader, so recording it goes through `proxies::for_publication` + `Index::publish_locked` rather than the raw `save_locked`, exactly as a migration's record does — the raw writer refuses a protocol move with existing commands rather than stranding them, and that refusal is what the first run measured. **(5) The walk is entered by the command the user typed and never by the installer underneath it.** `InstallRequest.recommends` is `false` by default, so a requirement install, an import replay, a resume and each recommendation of the walk itself never re-enter it; the walk enumerates the next level from the installed packages' own declarations, which is what makes «breadth-first in declaration order over a visited set» a loop rather than a recursion. **(6) One report row per reference, with its outcome, rather than three parallel arrays.** `AV-FMT-030` asked for `recommended[]`, `skipped[]` and `suggested[]` on `[format.cli-install-report]`; as built the first two are one `recommended[]` of rows carrying `installed | satisfied | skipped | planned` with an optional `reason`, and they land on `[format.cli-application-report]` and `[format.cli-application-plan]` — the documents the application plane actually emits — because `cli-install-report`'s root already has a `skipped` member that means skipped **slots**, and because every skip reason the record lists (not an app, no option for this platform, unsatisfiable, not carried, install failed) is an application-plane reason. `--plan-only` fills the same rows with `planned`, so the plan and the report are one shape read twice. **(7) The project home's consent gate is honoured by narrowing, not by widening.** `#APP-RECOMMENDS-CONSENT` requires that a recommendation be checked by the same gate as its recommender; that gate reads the **lock's** app rows (`crates/vibe-cli/src/commands/app/project.rs`) and a recommendation is not one, so rather than inventing a second gate the walk is **not entered at all** on the project-home plane unless the run already carries explicit consent (`--assume-yes` / `--unattended`). That is strictly stronger than the gate: without consent nothing the user did not name is installed there, so a recommendation cannot be a way past a consent the direct request would have needed. **(8) `--no-recommends` is one invocation posture, carried as a decided answer.** It travels as the invocation context's resolved posture, then `InstallPolicy`, then `vibe_install::InstallRequest`, then `SourceSolveRequest.recommends` — beside the offline posture it sits next to and never re-derived — and the resolver seam gained `DepSolver::solve_without_recommends` (with the ordinary solve as the default, which is the honest answer for a cell that expands no weak dependency) plus the masked sibling, so a visibility re-solve cannot bring back what the first solve declined. The plan's file list named only the resolver branch; the posture's path through `vibe-package-source`, `vibe-install` and `vibe-orchestrator` is the part the list understated. **(9) The project plane's `[suggests]` line is the one clause not built, and the reason is the finding of `#WEAK-TODAY`.** `[format.cli-install-report]` is assembled from the boundary-measured `InstallProgress` and the slot rows, which carry no manifest, so a `suggested[]` there needs a new channel from the plan through `InstallRun`; and in the same breath the project plane's `[recommends]` is pruned by the effective-set projection, so the whole project-plane weak-dependency surface wants one deliberate pass — an owner decision about PROP-050 `#EFFECTIVE-SET` and a report channel together — rather than half of it now. The application plane's suggestion line, its `--json` member and its plan member are built and tested.

p.WEAK-OPEN: **Open, each with the default the design takes unless the owner says otherwise.** (W1) A failed recommended install leaves exit 0 on the install the user asked for; the default is yes, on the ground that a weak dependency whose failure fails the strong act is not weak. (W2) Transitive recommendations are followed with a visited set and no depth limit; the alternative is one level from the explicitly requested package, which is cheaper to reason about but differs from the project plane for no reason a user could name. (W3) A recommended application is installed **exposed**, not hidden: a recommended maven the user cannot run is pointless. The alternative — hidden, then exposed on first use — needs a mechanism that does not exist. (W4) The weak edge is one attribute on the existing requirer edge rather than a third scope beside `build` and `runtime`; the default is the attribute, because a scope decides where a requirement runs and a weak edge decides only whether removal is blocked.

p.changelog: 2026-11-10: implemented as campaign phase P7d, in four commits — the inventory generation, the global flag, the application plane's walk with its reports, and this record. `#WEAK-PURPOSE`, `#APP-RECOMMENDS`, `#APP-RECOMMENDS-MECHANICS`, `#APP-RECOMMENDS-CONSENT`, `#NO-RECOMMENDS-FLAG`, `#WEAK-FORMAT-CHANGES` and `#WEAK-OPEN` are `impl/done`; `#SUGGESTS-UNCHANGED` is `impl/work` for exactly one clause — the project plane's own suggestion line — and `#WEAK-TODAY` is corrected in place by a measurement the design had taken only at the solver seam. `#P7D-AS-BUILT` records the nine things the code decided. — 2026-11-10: adopted on the owner's decision of the same day, as the general-model half of the APP-VERSIONS P7 generalisation. `#WEAK-TODAY` records what ships; `#APP-RECOMMENDS`, `#APP-RECOMMENDS-MECHANICS` and `#APP-RECOMMENDS-CONSENT` settle the application plane; `#NO-RECOMMENDS-FLAG` settles the flag for every kind and states what it deliberately does not persist; `#SUGGESTS-UNCHANGED` gives the weaker level a report line and no behaviour; `#WEAK-FORMAT-CHANGES` points at the campaign's `AV-FMT` records. Four questions stay the owner's in `#WEAK-OPEN`. Nothing is implemented.
